newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG mercenaries fly home, turmoil remains.
newsitem.headline: PNG mercenaries fly home, turmoil remains.

text.p: Dozens of foreign mercenaries hired by Papua New Guinea to put down an island rebellion headed home on Friday, leaving behind them a nation in turmoil.
As armed police clamped down on fresh unrest, about 50 mercenaries flew out of Port Moresby airport -- expelled by the soldiers they were meant to have fought alongside.
Australian television said the mercenaries' leader, retired British colonel Tim Spicer, was among those who flew off.
Spicer, a former senior U.N. peacekeeper in Bosnia, is chief executive of British mercenary firm Sandline International.
On the fifth day of the crisis, protests spread to the country's main university and to the provinces although police managed to prevent any more street violence in the capital.
Keeping up the pressure, the sacked army commander gave embattled Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan and two senior ministers another deadline to quit.

"With a bit of commonsense and guidance from God, the prime minister and his two ministers will see the light and resign by next Tuesday," said the general, who still commands the loyalty of army rank-and-file and most officers.

The crisis in Papua New Guinea continued to preoccupy its neighbours. An Australian envoy met senior officials in Port Moresby and in Canberra Prime Minister John Howard said troops had been put on alert in case the situation worsened.

The worst crisis in PNG's 22-year history as an independent nation began on Monday when army chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok demanded that Chan quit over his hiring of Spicer's mercenaries to put down an uprising on Bougainville island.
Singirok was promptly sacked but on Friday, holed up inside the Murray Barracks, the general said Chan and two other senior ministers had to quit before parliament sits again next Tuesday.

"With a bit of commonsense and guidance from God, the prime minister and his two ministers will see the light and resign by next Tuesday," Singirok, guarded by a dozen loyal soldiers, told reporters in the garden of his residence.
At the airport the last mercenaries flew out on a chartered Air Guinea jet believed to be headed for Hong Kong.
Major Walter Enuma, who has played a key role in the army campaign against the mercenaries, escorted them onto the tarmac.
An onlooker held up a banner saying: "Tim Spicer you murderer get out of my country." Another banner read: "Sandline, piss off."
Around 1,000 students at Papua New Guinea University called off a march on parliament but gave the government a petition demanding Chan's resignation and Singirok's return.
There were reports of unrest in at least one provincial town. Local radio said police fired teargas at thousands of demonstrators in the northern town of Lae.
Singirok on Friday handed out copies of PNG's contract with Sandline, saying it was "unconstitutional, unlawful and against all general principles of humanity".
The contract showed that the mercenaries, mostly South African veterans, would have been used as frontline fighters and not -- as Chan has maintained -- as mere trainers.
The contract was worth a total of US$36 million, at least half of which has already been paid.
Suspending the contract on Thursday, Chan announced that he would set up a commission of inquiry into the contract.
Protesters dismissed the move, as did Singirok.
"We do not want a review," said one student leader. "Chan is a wily politician and he is just trying to water down the situation."
